sources.title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
sources.summary: Political tension grips France after rioting marred protests over the cost of living and struggling public services, Katya Adler writes.
sources.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, President Emmanuel Macron urged calm in his national address following widespread looting and violence By Katya Adler Europe editor ,Â Reporting from Paris Published 28 minutes ago France's Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history. On Saturday over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared. An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously. There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished. Macron's speech has been roundly criticised on social media forums and by political opponents for lacking concrete detail. How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account? How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time? Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated? And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education? Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Vandals defaced Statue de la Republique in central Paris over the weekend On Sunday the Secretary General of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, accused Macron of failing to address students' concerns, the cost-of-living crisis or the dwindling quality of public services in France. He's apparently passed that baton to Prime Minister Lecornu. Yet he and his interior minister are charged by many in France with being woefully ill-prepared and under-policed ahead of Saturday's multiple, scheduled protests. The president of France's lower house of parliament, YaÃ«l Braun-Pivet, says she wants to open an inquiry into exactly what happened this weekend and why. "Things are dark in the city of light [a nickname for Paris]" was the graffiti I read daubed in red paint across a wall adjacent to a row of shattered shops in the French capital on Sunday night. Macron is widely viewed here as a lame-duck president. He is on his way out. There's a hotly contested race under way to become his successor, with the vote scheduled in six months' time. The presidential candidate from the anti-immigration nationalist right (Marine Le Pen) and also the anti-capitalist left (Jean-Luc Melenchon) are vying to make headlines. That is adding to current tensions in France - in politics as well as on the streets. Parliament here is paralysed, deeply divided between three vying political blocks. Then there are France's financial woes too. Investors are leaning hard on this country to get its spiralling public debt under control. But the French government worries, if it cuts public services or welfare, yet more angry people will pour out onto the streets. What now, what next, is our country broken? You hear these questions a lot at the moment. People across France were shocked and troubled by Saturday's events. The images of tear-gassed towns, apparently unimpeded looters and burning public buildings have worried the nation. Figure caption, 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight Many passers-by I speak to express frustration that, while they worry about the future, their leading politicians seem, instead, to be passionately focused on finger-pointing; blaming one another for the volatility. "While we worry for our safety, they use this situation as a pre-presidential election political football," teacher and father of three Edouard told me. Macron and his prime minister blamed Saturday's violent chaos on radical far left groups and delinquents; hard left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon alleged government "incompetence"; Marine Le Pen on the nationalist right, which likes to be seen as strong on law and order, posted a video seated in front of the French flag, giving a presidential-style address blaming the "Macronist administration that is out of steam, exhausted, and disoriented". For the next two weeks, the French authorities hope for a bit of a respite. Students start their half-term break as of Monday. But on 5 November, a cross-section of trade unions, plus France's disparate "yellow jacket" (gilets jaunes) movement that staged demonstrations for over a year in 2018 - during Macron's first term as president - have announced huge protests. France is holding its breath. sources.title: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to 'public benefit fund'
sources.summary: The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a blockbuster stock market listing.
sources.text: Image source, SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Image caption, Jack Clark, a co-founder and Head of Public Benefit of Anthropic By Peter Hoskins Business reporter Published 19 October 2026, 03:41 BST Updated 14 minutes ago Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good". The announcement comes as Anthropic lays the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (Â£750bn). The AI industry has come under intense scrutiny recently over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and the economy. Anthropic reportedly said in its initial public offering (IPO) filing that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity". Anthropic said its proposed fund could support nonprofit organisations, and efforts to address AI's impact on the jobs market. None of the shares held by the the fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas, it added. Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion, the Claude developer said in a statement released on Sunday. Technology billionaire Elon Musk responded to the announcement on social media with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." "This is what I will be doing," he added. Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (Â£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September. In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models. Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption. Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI , with that figure rising as high as â60% in advanced economies. In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity. "I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said. Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry. The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this. The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development. Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document , making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology. Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity. Since then, the president has named the director of national intelligence Jay Clayton as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will co-ordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations". Foto: Yle / Mapcreator Här är fastighetsköpen som Finland stoppat – Sverige saknar liknande lag Uppdaterad idag 05:47 Publicerad idag 05:44 Fastigheter nära kritisk infrastruktur, osannolika affärsplaner och köpare med kopplingar till rysk elit. Finland har stoppat 68 fastighetsaffärer sedan 2022 med hänvisning till säkerhetsrisker. I Sverige hade köpen sannolikt genomförts. SVT Nyheter har tidigare berättat att svenska myndigheter saknar en generell möjlighet att stoppa utländska fastighetsköp , med hänvisning till nationell säkerhet. Trots varningar från Säpo och nästan tio års utredning. Frågan har blivit aktuell i Sverige sedan Försvarsmakten velat ta över en fritidsfastighet nära en marinbas i Stockholms skärgård. I Finland ser det annorlunda ut. Landet har skärpt sina regler för fastighetsköp av utländska medborgare, utanför EU. ”Vi kommer inte tillåta affärer om det inte går att utesluta ett hot mot den nationella säkerheten”, säger försvarsminister Antti Häkkänen till Yle . Totalförbud för ryssar Fram till den 1 september i år har 68 fastighetsaffärer stoppats i Finland. Sedan juli 2025 råder dessutom i princip förbud för ryska och belarusiska medborgare att köpa fastigheter. Enligt Rickard Lindholm, sakkunnig på finska försvarsministeriet, handlar det om att förebygga säkerhetshot. Ryska staten kan tvinga medborgare utomlands att agera i Rysslands intresse. – Vi vill förhindra att det på lång sikt uppstår ett massivt fastighetsägarskap som skulle kunna användas i en eventuell konflikt. Stoppar inte rätt personer De finska lagarna fyller en viktig funktion enligt Kari Liuhto, professor i underrättelseforskning vid Finlands försvarshögskola. Misstänkta köp kan stoppas i ett tidigt skede. Att använda expropriering är både svårare och mer kostsamt, säger han. Men samtidigt anser han att lagarna fokuserar för mycket på medborgarskap. – I de flesta fall stoppar vi inte rätt personer, konstaterar Kari Liuhto. Enligt honom använder rysk underrättelsetjänst mellanhänder, eller andra metoder, om den vill komma över en strategiskt viktig fastighet. – De flesta ryska fastighetsköp i Finland har inget med underrättelseverksamhet att göra. Risken ökar Finska myndigheter är medvetna om risken för köp via bulvaner, och att den risken ökat sedan ett år tillbaka, när ryska köp stoppas helt. – Vi har möjligheter att ingripa mot misstänkta bulvaner, men utmaningen är att hitta dem, konstaterar Rickard Lindholm på finska försvarsministeriet. Trots luckor i lagstiftningen anser han att säkerhetshotande fastighetsköp ändå försvåras, eftersom köp granskas. – Den avskräckande effekten är det mest centrala. sources.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
sources.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.
sources.text: Figure caption, Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos By Monica Garnsey BBC Eye Published 4 hours ago Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia. One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil. He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs. The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland. Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves. He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow , Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was killed in Moscow last year by an explosive device hidden under his car There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities. The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself." And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out. The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this. There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024. It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify. Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine Two men tell of secret operations inside Russia. Watch on iPlayer Listen to the Podcast on BBC Sounds. If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube , external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome. "At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the warâ¦ Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says. His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets. "When these [drone] components are combinedâ¦ it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said. He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield. If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades. Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance. Image caption, Foma explained how he taught his undercover volunteers to trail Russian officers "You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers. Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information. He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets. "This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live. "In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points." He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints. Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals. "As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not." But he argued that his team's actions were justified. "I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared." Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves. Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule." But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance. Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event. Foma did his own digging on Ivan. After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year , external . One person was reported to have been killed in the incident. Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians. Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too. "The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said. To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside. Foma has the same rule for his operatives. "As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said. Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work. "Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said. Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands. Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities. So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return. Image caption, Marcin waiting to meet Ivan in Georgia - we were surprised by Ivan's apparent freedom to travel Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him. "You go to a third countryâ¦ where [Ukraine's] agents meet youâ¦ and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him. Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school". But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress. Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag. "There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holesâ¦ and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon. Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where. Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work. "Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia." But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change. "Putin won't live forever," he said. Related topics War in Ukraine Russia Ukraine Spying Drones

sources.title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
sources.summary: At least one person was killed in the strikes, which also hit a data centre used by Russia's equivalent of Facebook.
sources.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The St Petersburg Oil Terminal was among targets hit in the city overnight By Aleks Phillips Published 18 October 2026 At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities. The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five. A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit. Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week. Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing. It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel. Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July . Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday. St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed. He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible. Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning. Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire. It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes". As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions. Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections. Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort. Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism , including from some US Republicans. However, on Sunday, Zelensky said on Telegram he had had conversations with Trump's top negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. He said their teams are in constant communication and preparing the next diplomatic steps. Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year. Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years. Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter. Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said. METR, a nonprofit that has worked with leading labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems. A greater role for third-party evaluators is among the main concrete steps the labs have proposed in response to rising concern about the dangers more capable AI systems could pose to the economy, cyber security and humanity at large. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei achieved a rare moment of unity with arch-rivals Sam Altman and Elon Musk in September when the OpenAI and SpaceX bosses rallied behind his proposal to embed external auditors in the leading labs. Thursday’s announcement marks the first step to implementing these pledges. OpenAI has yet to lay out plans to bring in evaluators after Altman said Amodei’s proposals were a good idea. “As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessment,” Anthropic said on Thursday. “We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work.” Critics of Anthropic’s proposal to use evaluators have argued the arrangements could lead to conflicts of interest, pointing to issues in the accounting sector, and that greater government regulation is required. Anthropic argued that sharing information publicly could benefit malicious actors or competitors and added that its evaluators will operate similarly to bank supervision, whereby regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. “If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance,” the company said. Anthropic is also under pressure to reassure investors that safety issues will not overshadow its initial public offering, expected this year at a more than $2tn valuation. It devoted a large part of investor presentations this week to laying out its safety practices. METR was one of the organisations that investigated the hack of Hugging Face by rogue OpenAI models, reviewing thousands of logs and receiving company laptops. Anthropic has now onboarded six METR employees, giving them company hardware, office space and “access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to.” The lab said it has encouraged employees to share information with the evaluators as they would with a fellow employee working in risk. Anthropic is not paying METR for this arrangement. The research group does not accept donations from AI companies or their staff. It is funded by donations from individuals and philanthropic organisations, as well as government bodies such as the UK’s AI Security Institute. The evaluators will publish their analysis, and Anthropic cannot veto publication. However, it can require them to redact information that falls into certain categories, such as customer data, details covered by attorney-client privilege or information about model architectures. Anthropic added it was still working with Accenture, which was named a partner on safety testing last month, with each committing at least $1 billion to set up new safeguards. Another third-party tester is SecureBio, which reviews chemical and biological weapon risk for the company. “We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same,” Anthropic said. METR said: “We stand ready to work with all frontier AI developers to bring better evidence to the public.” © 2026 The Financial Times Ltd . sources.title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
sources.summary: There were violent clashes between demonstrators and riot police throughout Saturday in the capital Tirana.
sources.text: Figure caption, Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on Saturday By Nick Thorpe Correspondent ,Â Reporting from Tirana, Albania Published 17 October 2026 Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row. Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests. The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time. Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement , with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration. Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street. The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday. During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard. Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days. Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic. Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyes Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon. As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police. Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation. The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris. George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes. He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June. In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police. Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too. "We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in Franceâ¦ we are trying to make a revolution. "Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence." Image caption, Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana. She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights." She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations. Image caption, Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades. The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative? Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections". The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join. In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things". He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030. He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity. Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule. Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni. She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest. Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services, Albanian media reported. Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups. Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions. "Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC. "He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances." Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029. sources.title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
sources.summary: Research suggests listening more while talking less. Killing aimless meetings can help, too.
sources.text: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives. Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior. Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect , communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior . As a graduate student, Kreamer was interested in studying teamwork, leadership, and work relationships. During her doctorate work with meeting scientist Steven Rogelberg, she realized that meetings would be a fine venue for studying all of that and more. “You can use a meeting as a stage to study anything you want,” she says. After all, at their core “meetings are a fundamental aspect of how we organize and interact as social beings,” Kreamer and coauthors Rogelberg and Jon Gray, both of the University of North Carolina in Charlotte, wrote in the 2026 article. To tap meetings for study, researchers typically use two approaches. The first is a classic survey in which researchers retroactively ask people about their real or simulated meeting experiences and analyze the responses. The second method is to analyze specific behaviors and trends extracted from audio and video recordings of meetings. Such precise content is “where the music is,” says industrial and organizational psychologist Nale Lehmann-Willenbrock, director of the Center for Better Work at the University of Hamburg, Germany. In one experiment, Lehmann-Willenbrock and colleagues extracted data from video-recorded meetings to study how leader communication affects team interaction during decision-making. The researchers found that respectful, attentive inquiry by meeting leaders enhanced team performance , in contrast to when leaders asked questions but didn’t attentively listen to responses. Leading with listening As with many meeting science studies, their findings about what improves meetings’ effectiveness often seem obvious, but meeting researchers note that meetings often stray far from these ideals. Such research also consistently reveals the importance of active listening, says Lehmann-Willenbrock: not just passive acknowledgement by the listener but actively providing thoughtful feedback. In virtual meetings, because “we’ve all learned to mute ourselves if we’re not talking, very often, active listening is killed completely.” The balance of listening and speaking also can influence how well a meeting goes. Meeting leaders and participants may retain very different views of whether a meeting was successful, notes Lehmann-Willenbrock. “Often, leaders talk the most, which is also why they often think their meetings are pretty good,” she says. Kreamer also emphasizes that it’s important that meeting leaders lead but not dominate the discussion. Leaders should monitor the proportion of time they are speaking to allow for inclusion of many voices. Research supports a checklist of additional things that leaders can do before, during, and after a meeting to make it a success, says Lehmann-Willenbrock. To set the stage, leaders should choose appropriate rooms, refreshments, and lighting, invite only those who need to be there, plan to start and end on time, prepare an agenda, set and communicate clear goals, and allow time for pre-meeting conversation. Socializing first, especially in virtual meetings, is beneficial, Lehmann-Willenbrock says. Her research has shown that “for more introverted participants and more quiet participants, this warmup phase is really helpful because it helps them make more active contributions inside the meeting.” Indeed, her studies on face-to-face meetings have shown that pre-meeting small talk predicts meeting effectiveness, particularly for more introverted participants. But pre-meeting talk is rare in virtual meetings; she says leaders should consider establishing a norm of arriving early or using the first few minutes for an informal check-in. Engaging attendees Facilitators can increase the likelihood of a successful meeting by making sure all opinions are heard. Kreamer recommends a technique called silent brainstorming to get all participants, even shy and reluctant ones, to engage in idea generation. It involves creating a shared virtual space, such as a chat or online document, to which all participants contribute simultaneously. Kreamer points to a 2009 study that found this approach (some researchers call it “brainwriting”) was more effective than traditional free-for-all spoken brainstorming in meetings. Kreamer uses this technique when she and her students are dreaming up research ideas in class. “We can all see each other working,” she says, and the quieter students don’t worry about interrupting or having to verbally express their suggestions. After 10 minutes, she reviews the ideas with the group. Zofia Walters, a doctoral student in industrial organizational psychology working with Kreamer, has been studying another aspect of meeting inclusiveness: the needs of neurodiverse participants. Her studies provide evidence that while practices like minimizing distractions, documenting instructions, using shared calendars, and building regular check-ins into meetings likely benefit all employees, they may be especially helpful for people with ADHD. In a survey of 147 employees from a variety of workplaces, Walters asked participants about their most recent virtual meeting: how effective it was, how fatigued they felt afterward and their emotional state. Participants also reported how much time they spent multitasking during the meeting, such as by answering emails, and how long their camera was on. They also shared whether they had an ADHD diagnosis, either formal or informal (based on self-assessment). In findings yet to be published, Walters reported that individuals with ADHD were more likely to report feeling more meeting fatigue, especially when the camera was on for extended periods, than non-ADHD peers. They also reported poorer emotional states. Her findings also suggest that multitasking during meetings may help ADHD attendees manage boredom or hyperactivity. Effective meeting practices don’t end when the meeting ends. After a meeting, leaders can ensure it was time well spent by communicating action items to participants, taking concrete steps to implement the ideas and tasks generated in the meeting, and assessing employee engagement, meeting satisfaction, and meeting effectiveness, Lehmann-Willenbrock and colleagues concluded in a 2018 paper in Organizational Dynamics . The downsides—and upsides Does all this time spent in meetings take a toll on workers? The evidence seems to suggest so. Research has found that employees anticipate feeling worse and being less productive when their day is jam-packed with meetings, especially when they are working on complex tasks. Meetings are sometimes seen as the default way to get things done, but often, people don’t specify what they want to achieve from them, says cognitive scientist Ava Scott of the University of Copenhagen. This, she says, “makes a lot of meetings feel very purposeless.” Recurring meetings tend to be the most aimless, Scott’s research on Microsoft employees has found; one participant described the content of these successive meets as dreamlike in their similarity to one another. If there’s no clear goal, you don’t know why you’re meeting, and everyone’s very busy, it probably indicates that taking up people’s time with a meeting isn’t ideal, says Scott. Kreamer notes that some companies, such as Shopify, have cut all recurring meetings. Nevertheless, a 2026 study of more than 9,000 workers in Norway found that while meetings are both common and costly, their benefits may make them worth enduring. The research, led by economist David Deming at Harvard University and based on data collected by Norwegian survey company Norstat, found that meeting intensity is positively associated with subsequent wage growth and on-the-job learning. One possible explanation for the finding is that these meetings may offer the chance to interact with more senior colleagues and so enable the transmission of key knowledge. The important caveat is that the study, published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, was correlational, so it can’t establish a causal relationship between the number of meetings attended and wage increases; it does further suggest that although the cost of meetings is particularly high for high-wage companies, the benefits may be even higher. That leads the authors to conclude: “Meetings are the broccoli of work—widely disliked, but probably good for us anyway.” Strategies for success Humor can help make a meeting successful—as long as it’s authentic, supportive, or positive rather than demeaning. Used appropriately, humor can spur new ideas and enhance team performance. This is most likely to work when meeting participants are well-acquainted, Lehmann-Willenbrock reported after analyzing videos of meetings at two German companies. People have to know each other well enough to feel safe making a joke, she says. But not everyone is comfortable using humor in meetings, says science educator and comedian Vita Stout, now at Sierra College in Rocklin, California. The former bat researcher attended the International Congress for Bat Research in Austin, Texas, in 2022, and took notes on the jokes being used in meeting talks—transcribing exact quotes, their timing, and audience response. Stout’s research, coauthored with bat scientists and published in the Proceedings of Biological Sciences B , argued that when well-timed and used appropriately, humor in scientific meetings can be a tool for connection and community-building. But joke-telling was more prominent among meeting participants with privilege and power, with older, well-established male scientists making jokes more frequently than early career researchers and scientists from underrepresented groups. As in comedy, timing is also key when planning meetings. Scheduling should consider the human circadian rhythm and avoid meeting during the after-lunch energy dip. Lehmann-Willenbrock admits ruefully that her own academic environment often doesn’t obey that rule. “A lot of our committee meetings are scheduled when people are at their most tired,” she says, or digesting lunch. It’s also important to be mindful of people’s work and family obligations in meeting scheduling. “I have two small kids,” she says, “and I always get really angry when a meeting gets called that’s about something… diversity- or inclusion-related, and then it’s scheduled at 5 pm.” Some research suggests there are cultural differences in basic expectations for meetings . In a survey of 1,432 workers from six countries, for example, Lehmann-Willenbrock and collaborators measured how frustrated, irritated, and upset individuals became in imagined scenarios in which leaders or other participants showed up five, 10, or 15 minutes late to meetings. Respondents from the United States and the Netherlands were especially perturbed by a late leader and a high degree of lateness. People from China and Chile weren’t so frustrated by the same situations. There are very few cross-cultural studies like this in the world of meeting science, says Kreamer. “We have these best practices of meetings that we’ve learned over the past 30 years,” she says, but the bulk of studies have come out of Europe or North America. That’s a deficit she’d like to see addressed to see whether the same rules for optimal meeting success apply. As soon as those results are out, we’ll have to call another meeting. sources.title: Why BioWare's Neverwinter Nights still has thousands of active players
sources.summary: The single-player is just OK, but according to the players, that doesn't matter.
sources.text: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav C:\ArsGames We love games here at the Ars Orbiting HQ, from modern to ancient and all points in between. With that in mind, we’ve partnered with the folks at GOG.com to create a store page featuring a curated list of some of our favorites from GOG’s catalog . From time to time, we’ll rotate a couple of titles off the list and add a few new ones; altogether, we have about 50 games to set before you. Usually at least once a month, we’ll publish a personal retrospective like this one, where we’ll feature one of the games from the list—perhaps a retro game you’ve heard of, perhaps a modern title you missed. Regardless, GOG will have a DRM-free version of the game ready to go. Be sure to check out the earlier pieces in the series ! Neverwinter Nights was made by the studio that produced seminal RPGs Baldur’s Gate , Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic , Mass Effect , and Dragon Age . It sold well and was critically acclaimed at launch. Yet, somehow, it has not been canonized in most gamers’ minds over the decades the same way the games that came before and after it were. Nonetheless, more than two decades later, it still has a tight-knit and surprisingly active community that none of those other games can rival. I think that’s partly because it was a completely different beast. BioWare is known for making multi-character, story-driven role-playing games that focused primarily on single-player story campaigns, though some supported co-op play in those campaigns. With Neverwinter Nights , BioWare instead made a game that was as focused on a modding toolset for content creation as it was on giving players a pre-packaged story, and that emphasized multiplayer at least as much as solo play. Today you would expect this to be a calculated attempt to bring more long-term, always-on, multiplayer-as-a-service to an RPG franchise that has mostly appealed to solo players. You might imagine it would be about selling cosmetics, a subscription, or a battle pass, or maybe you would think it was about nabbing appealing engagement numbers. But it’s clear from playing it today that Neverwinter Nights wasn’t primarily made for those reasons. Instead, it came from a passion for tabletop role-playing and a desire to get closer to that in video game form than ever before. Yes, the BioWare team noted in some interviews that they saw this as a trial run for exploring the idea of making a massively multiplayer game (MMO)—something that, in the year 2000, was seen by many as the hot new business opportunity in gaming, and which was in many ways the precursor to the games-as-a-service we see today. They then indicated they realized that an MMO was harder to make than they had assumed and abandoned that ambition well before Neverwinter Nights shipped. Neverwinter Nights is not exactly an MMO. Instead, it’s designed for small communities of people to inhabit and create with, and it features a powerful toolset for virtual dungeon masters to use to subject regular players to challenges in an improvisational way on a live server. “We always envisioned it as a table with four legs—the single player, the multiplayer, the DMing tools and the toolset (the module making tools),” BioWare’s Ray Muzyka told IGN around the time the game was released. “They all appeal to different groups, and we’ve tried to make them all equivalently high quality.” Over the past month, I’ve been replaying Neverwinter Nights ‘ main story campaign, The Wailing Death, as a solo player, for the first time in 20 years. The nostalgia has been strong in this replay, but I have also found that BioWare didn’t quite nail “equivalently high quality” for all the pillars. Still, it doesn’t matter, because as we’ll see when we check in with the game’s community, the campaign is not the point. Table of Contents Jump to section The single-player experience is… fine “The single player experience has to be as good as anything we’ve ever done in [ Baldur’s Gate ], [ Baldur’s Gate 2 ], or Throne of Bhaal and hopefully better,” Muzyka told IGN. “Our goal here at BioWare is that each game we do has to be better than the previous one.” If single-player is one of the legs, it might be fair to call Neverwinter Nights ‘ table a little wobbly. It still stands, but you know how irritating it can be. For example, Neverwinter Nights leaves behind Baldur’s Gate or Icewind Dale ‘s party-based systems, and instead has the player controlling just one character directly. It makes sense for a multiplayer game, but doesn’t work as well for a single-player experience in this case—at least with the Dungeons & Dragons rules of the time. I chose to play a monk, a martial arts specialist, simply because I’ve always been drawn to that particular fantasy identity, and because I’d never played one in a D&D game. I regretted that decision after a while. For many of the character levels covered in The Wailing Death, the monk basically just picks between two fighting modes: one that misses more but attacks more frequently, and one that’s just normal. That, along with some intense restrictions on which weapons or armor can be used while keeping all their benefits, and a couple of knockdown and stun attacks that often don’t work, make up the whole kit for many hours of playtime, particularly in the first act. (It does get better later on, though.) The original campaign is fun and nostalgic, but it’s arguably not BioWare’s best. Credit: GOG The original campaign is fun and nostalgic, but it’s arguably not BioWare’s best. Credit: GOG A kit like this makes sense in a pen-and-paper RPG with a live dungeon master (DM), because the player and DM can work together to invent creative expressions of their abilities, and it works in a party in a video game because it’s just one of multiple complementary characters with a wide range of skills and spells. But for a game that is about 80 percent battling enemies without controlling any other characters, it gets monotonous quickly. There aren’t as many meaningful character builds, gearing, or tactical choices as you’re used to in some other RPGs until quite a ways into the campaign. Often, you just run in and watch the dice roll until either you die or the enemy dies, while sometimes drinking potions. This problem is less severe with some other classes, but the tension is usually there to some degree. Whereas Baldur’s Gate 2 , for example, had a partial authored background for your character that then played into the narrative, Neverwinter Nights leaves you as an Elder Scrolls-like blank slate. I normally love that ! It’s good for role-playing with friends, because you can make up your own character completely. But it means the story can’t be character-driven, and the gameplay doesn’t provide enough flexibility or freedom in return. Still, I enjoyed my experience with the campaign when I replayed it recently, even if it couldn’t match Baldur’s Gate 2 , Knights of the Old Republic , Mass Effect , or other BioWare classics for me personally. While the story wasn’t anything special by BioWare’s standards, there was something genuinely cozy to me about the genericness of the narrative. It took me back to an earlier time in CRPGs, before things got quite so precious. “This is just like D&D !” was still enough to sell it on its own. Maybe it’s just nostalgia, though. Since most people played the game solo, and it was a relatively small portion of the player base that dove deep into the construction kit or DM tools, I think this is the main reason Neverwinter Nights has not achieved the same pantheon status as other BioWare titles that came before and after it. But for those lucky few who were invested in those other table legs, it actually was quite special—and amazingly, it remains so today. The persistent worlds of Neverwinter Nights “The main thing I would shout from the rooftops if I could, is that firing up Neverwinter Nights and launching its original campaign… does not do justice to what Neverwinter Nights has become since,” a longtime player named Daniel Morris told me. He goes by Irongron in the community, and he runs Arelith , which is both one of the OG persistent multiplayer servers and one of the most popular servers today. Morris is also working on a visual overhaul of the original campaign; he hopes to release it next year. Arelith hit its peak player count “a little less than two years ago,” as Morris tells it—not way back when the game was new. “Our community is the heart of Arelith, it’s not just our audience, but where we find our DMs and developers,” he said. Arelith is a fountain of creativity; for example, this is original artwork commissioned for the game’s loading screens from artist Matheus Graef. Credit: Matheus Graef Arelith is a fountain of creativity; for example, this is original artwork commissioned for the game’s loading screens from artist Matheus Graef. Credit: Matheus Graef I spent many evenings in my younger days playing multi-user dungeons (MUDs), the text-based online role-playing games that preceded MMOs like EverQuest or World of Warcraft . While there were big MUDs, many were small communities of just one or two dozen people, and often, those same people were the ones actually making the game’s content. For example, I was a room builder for one MUD; I wrote the descriptions for places in the MUD’s world and decided which monsters, NPCs, or items inhabited those places. Neverwinter Nights ‘ multiplayer platform and community—both as it was back in the 2000s and as it is today—reminds me of those MUD days. There’s an ownership of that shared world that is entirely lost in the MMO days, perhaps more akin to a modern, small Minecraft server than an MMO with thousands of users. That seems to be part of the appeal for a player I spoke with who goes by the name NelaK in the community, and who has, among other things, taken over maintenance and moderation of the Neverwinter Vault , the community’s de facto hub for two decades. The website hosts news, patches, assets, mods, a forum, a wiki, and an associated Discord server. “It’s not an MMO, and that’s a good thing in my opinion. The communities are smaller, which means your roleplay and your actions matter and can affect the world,” said NelaK. “The world itself can be tailored around what the players want. That’s a unique thing that you can’t get from an MMO or from smaller-scale multiplayer games. It sits in a sweet spot where you can have enough players that it feels like a proper community and a world you can engage with while you can still matter.” Baldur’s Gate and Icewind Dale did have multiplayer, where each player could control one or more characters directly. As noted, Neverwinter Nights limits each player to one character, but it adds a new role: a dungeon master, who can spawn enemies, occupy and act as NPCs, and more, to aid in group storytelling, similar to a pen-and-paper game. “While Arelith is essentially a mini MMO, many of the other servers pride themselves in running highly curated, beautifully crafted campaign worlds much closer to tabletop role-playing game emulator that Neverwinter Nights was first intended as,” Morris told me. He called Neverwinter Nights “a direct translation of the tabletop role-playing game experience into the digital sphere.” It’s as much a construction kit as it is a game The game’s modding kit and easy-to-use scripting tools let players build scenarios relatively quickly. It essentially let players build a little RPG world, run it, and inhabit it. It was a bustling scene back then, and there’s still a community doing this today. The combination of the relative simplicity of the graphics and the elegance of the tools make this toolset an unusually excellent balance between flexible, powerful, and easy to learn. “The tile-based areas are basic and limiting in some respects, but they do mean that building areas is quick and easy,” explained NelaK. “It’s much more approachable than a lot of other platforms.” For NelaK and some other members of the game’s community today, the game’s tools aren’t just the remaining appeal—they’re the main appeal. “I’ve been playing Neverwinter Nights since launch day. I remember one of my friends dragging me along to the store because they really wanted the game and I went just to keep them company,” he remembered. “I ended up buying it, and I’ve been hooked ever since, but to this day, I’ve still never played through the original campaigns… and yet I’ve played Neverwinter Nights or spent time building or working on something Neverwinter Nights -related most days since.” I toyed around with the tools quite a bit back in the day. I remember re-creating a big chunk of the world of my favorite MMO at the time, Meridian 59 , with the intent to make a story-driven, single-player campaign for that game; Meridian 59 had very little narrative as it was. I also remember that Neverwinter Nights was for many years a common way for would-be narrative designers to make a portfolio piece for applying for jobs within the games industry. When I was in college, a close friend of mine (Brian “Psychochild” Green, who at the time co-ran Meridian 59 , and sadly has since passed) offered to show my Neverwinter Nights modules to some friends of his at BioWare if I wanted to interview for a job there to write for their next game, which, based on timing, probably would have been Mass Effect . I declined in order to focus on other priorities I had at the time, for better or worse. Similarly, many (though certainly not all) people in the community have professional backgrounds closely related to, or at least adjacent to, game development. “ Neverwinter Nights provides a unique intersection of where I can apply my technical and professional skills along with my interest in video games and do it for something that doesn’t feel like work,” said N

sources.summary: Franske världstvåan Felix Lebrun blev för svår. Anton Källberg förlorade en tajt EM-final – efter att ha blivit utklassad i det avgörande skiljesetet. – Det kändes bra, förutom i de två sista seten då jag är i princip chanslös, säger en besviken silvermedaljör till SVT.

Anton Källberg förlorade en tajt EM-final – efter att ha blivit utklassad i det avgörande skiljesetet. – Det kändes bra, förutom i de två sista seten då jag är i princip chanslös, säger en besviken silvermedaljör till SVT. Tidigare under söndagen skrällvann Anton Källberg mot tyske världselvan Dang Qiu i semifinalen. Frågan var om den svenske 29-åringen skulle orka ladda om till finalen bara några timmar senare mot storfavoriten och världstvåan, fransmannen Felix Lebrun, 20. Svaret var ja. Källberg spelade fokuserat och tog hem det första setet med 11–7. Redan i andra set tvingande Källberg den unge fransmannen att förbruka sin timeout efter att ha tagit fyra raka bollar vid ställningen 10–5 till Lebrun. ”Timen” gav dock effekt och Lebrun skrek ut sin glädje efter setvinst med 11–9. ”Hur stark är han mentalt?!” Källberg, rankad 29:a i världen, spelade varierat och överraskade Lebrun flera gånger med långa servar. Trots att svensken spelade bra pingis vann Felix Lebrun det efterföljande setet med 13–11. Men Källberg reste sig återigen och kvitterade till 2–2 i set. – Hur stark är han mentalt?! frågar sig J-O Waldner retoriskt i SVT:s sändning. Finalen utvecklade sig till en förstaklassens nagelbitare. Källberg tog hem det femte setet med 11–9 och var bara ett set från ett historiskt EM-guld. Nära första svenska guldet på 26 år 2000 vann Peter Karlsson EM-guld i Bremen. Sedan dess har inte en svensk herrspelare vunnit EM i singel – och nu hade Källberg chansen att ta det första svenska EM-guldet på 26 år. Men, med kniven mot strupen gjorde Felix Lebrun sina två överlägset bästa set i matchen och vann de två avslutande seten med 11–6 och 11–1. ”Ska vara jättestolt” Anton Källberg åker från Slovenien med två EM-silver. I går förlorade han dubbelfinalen i par med Kristian Karlsson mot Felix och Alexis Lebrun. – På förhand hade man tagit två silvermedaljer, men just nu är det tråkigt. Det hade varit så fint med ett guld, säger Källberg. – Fantastiskt. Första singelfinalen och han står upp här och det har varit tuffa matcher hela vägen. Han har jobbat stenhårt från början av turneringen till nu. Han ska vara jättestolt över det han gör här, sammanfattar den svenska förbundskaptenen Michael Maze Anton Källbergs EM. Damernas final vanns av ryskan Elizabet Abraamian efter att hon besegrat tyskan Annett Kaufmann med 4–3 i set. Sabah Göranson från Älvsjö besökte på söndagen platsen för att lämna en blomma. – Det är fruktansvärt att ytterligare en människa förlorar sitt liv på det här sättet, i en skjutning. Jag kände att jag måste gå ut och visa att jag bryr mig, säger hon. Sabah Göranzon beskriver Kämpetorpshallarna som en plats där det brukar vara fullt med barn och ungdomar, liv och rörelse. I dag är stämningen annorlunda. Hon tycker att det är extra obehagligt när våldet tar sig in på fotbollsplaner och idrottshallar. – Jag är jättetrött på att läsa om sådana här händelser. Mina barn är engagerade i föreningar och jag med. När det drabbar människor som engagerar sig för barn och unga, det känns extra, säger hon. Suzan Habib som bor i området beskriver den första känslan som oro och chock. – Jag börjar tänka på min egen tonåring som nyss gått på den skolan. Så det känns ju väldigt nära, säger hon när hon besöker platsen. – Det här önskar man ju inte någon ungdom. Det är supertråkigt att de ska behöva vara med om det här, säger Suzan Habib. ”Hammarby Fotboll i sorg” Många unga var på plats i lokalerna på fredagskvällen eftersom det pågick en innebandymatch och en fotbollsmatch arrangerad av Hammarbys Samhällsmatchen, som beskrivs som Hammarbys samhällsprojekt. ”Flera anställda inom Hammarby Fotboll har arbetat tillsammans med henne och känner henne väl, och det är med stor bestörtning vi tagit emot beskedet”, skriver föreningen på Instagram . Föreningen skriver vidare att kvinnan tidigare varit en del av organisationen bakom Samhällsmatchen och att Hammarby Fotboll nu är en förening i sorg. ”Med anledning av detta kommer våra representationslag att spela med sorgband vid dagens respektive matcher i Obos Damallsvenskan och Allsvenskan”. Arbetade i stadsdelens ungdomsverksamhet Efter det ska kvinnan ha fortsatt arbete med unga i kommunen, något som stadsdelsdirektören kunde bekräfta under lördagen. – Personen var en medarbetare i vår ungdomsverksamhet. Det är en fruktansvärd händelse och alla våra tankar går till familjen, anhöriga och medarbetarna i vår organisation, säger Lee Orberson, stadsdelsdirektör i Hägersten-Älvsjö. Under söndagen kommer Stockholm stad fortsatt ha fritidsgården i Älvsjö öppen för krissamtal mellan 15 till 22.
